title: NYC Restaurant Inspections
subtitle: DOHMH violation citations, active NYC restaurants only

source.publisher: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, via NYC OpenData
source.note: Pulled live from the SODA API on every rebuild. The watermark is the publisher's own last-modified stamp. We check it on every page of every request — if the dataset changes mid-pull, the build fails loudly instead of quietly blending two states.

grain.note: Three true counts, three different questions. 3.37 violations per inspection · 2.81 inspections per restaurant. Report a row count as a restaurant count and you're off by 9.5×.

charts.title: Restaurants that score worse get inspected more
charts.insight: More inspections, worse scores. The median climbs from 12 at one inspection to ~30 at six or more — and it repeats in every cuisine.
charts.form_why: Points beat a curve here. You can have 1 or 2 inspections, never 1.6, so we plot four computed points instead of fitting a line. The first version used a regression that ran out to x=8, where almost no restaurants exist — a correct least-squares fit, drawing a claim about data that isn't there.
charts.method: Median, not mean — the score tops out at 214 and outliers drag an average. n printed at every point. Nothing under n=25 is drawn: the line ends where the evidence ends. The citywide panel splits 4/5/6+ because n supports it there (207/57/25); the cuisine facets pool at 4+ because American has 2 restaurants at 6 inspections and Mexican has 1.
charts.caution: The x-axis is the OUTCOME of enforcement policy, not its cause. DOHMH's written rule: any initial inspection scoring ≥14 gets re-inspected. We measured it — restaurants that ever scored ≥14 average 1.69 inspections vs 1.04 for those that never did. Part of this correlation is built in by the rule.

charts.title: One dataset, two arguments
charts.insight: This is how you flip an outcome without touching a single number. Left panel: Brooklyn is flat (+0.00). Right panel: BROOKLYN SURGES. Same query, same data, every axis labeled on both — and the right one still lies.
charts.form_why: Equal panels keep the tricks the only difference. An earlier version drew the spun panel narrower to keep the aspect-ratio trick — but then 'the y-axis is zoomed' blurred into 'the panel is squished', and the comparison was guilty of the thing it teaches.
charts.method: Left, the honest recipe: y from zero, window fixed by the question before looking, no smoothing, every line treated the same. Right, the spin recipe: y zoomed to Brooklyn's range, window cherry-picked for max slope out of 15 candidate starts, Brooklyn smoothed with a 3-month average while the other boroughs stay raw.
charts.caution: 'Read the axes' is the usual defense of a spun chart. It fails here: the window, the y-range, the aspect ratio and the one-sided smoothing have no axis labels. The frame does the lying.

charts.title: Queens is 'worst' — but per what?
charts.insight: Right claim, wrong evidence. Queens was called worst 'because it recorded the most critical violations' — but Manhattan has the most raw criticals (18,487 vs 13,253). Queens still leads both fair metrics, so the claim was right by accident. Rank walk: 2 → 1 → 1.
charts.form_why: A bump chart is a rank flip, drawn — and this claim was about rank. The leftmost column is the claimant's own metric on purpose; each step to the right divides their evidence by something fairer.
charts.method: Raw count → per 100 inspections → per restaurant, last 12 complete months. Values print at every node because rank alone hides how big the gaps are. The caption comes from the cluster shape, not the global range, so 'rank 1' and 'modest lead' can't contradict each other on the same image.
charts.caution: Neither way of dividing is automatically fairer. Per-inspection carries enforcement policy inside it. Per-restaurant mixes in how long each place has been open. What you divide by has to follow the decision you're making.

charts.title: The map, demoted to what a map can say
charts.insight: The pattern isn't on the map. A stakeholder asked for a map titled 'where frequent inspections cause worse outcomes' — but 98% of the link has nothing to do with geography. Pooled slope +5.75, zip-demeaned slope +5.64: neighborhoods explain 2%.
charts.form_why: We map the leftovers, not the raw pattern. A colored-in map of the raw link would show 'where' for a pattern that isn't about place. So each dot is severity minus its cuisine and neighborhood averages — only what geography still explains after those are stripped out. It renders as salt-and-pepper. That's the answer.
charts.method: 20,092 restaurants. 313 dropped for missing or (0,0) coordinates — dropped and counted. Aspect ratio set to ~cos(latitude) so NYC isn't stretched.
charts.caution: The requested title said 'cause' before any analysis had earned it. And here the arrow runs backward: risk-based enforcement sends more inspections to worse restaurants.

cannot_answer: Whether restaurants are actually cleaner or dirtier. Citations are what inspectors wrote down under a policy — not measurements of hygiene.

Anything about restaurants that failed and closed. Only ACTIVE restaurants are in the data — the failures were removed before we ever saw them. So 'do bad inspections predict closure' has no possible answer here.
Long-run trends. The data is a rolling window — roughly three years before each restaurant's most recent inspection. Any multi-year 'trend' is really the window moving.
Whether more inspections cause worse outcomes. The enforcement rule creates the correlation, and untangling it would take a controlled study — this data only watches; it can't run one.
